summary: Defines the procedure to register RTP payload formats as MIME subtypes for audio, video, and other media, so text-based protocols can name what is in an RTP stream. It also registers the payload formats from the RTP audio/video profile. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFCs 4855 and 4856.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP numbers its media types, so a number such as 0 means a format without saying which one. This RFC gives each of those formats a MIME type name, so that a protocol written in text can name what it is carrying. It also says how a MIME type and its parameters translate into the fields of a session description, and registers the formats from the standard audio and video profile.

questions: mime types for rtp payload formats
what is an rtp payload format
how does a mime type map to sdp
subtitle: Giving every RTP payload format a MIME type name, so text-based protocols can say what a stream carries.

tldr.problem: RTP identifies what it carries with a payload type number, which says nothing about the encoding itself. A text-based protocol, such as a session description or a control channel, had no standard way to name the format behind that number.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a procedure for registering each RTP payload format as a MIME subtype, with parameters for the clock rate, channel count and packet timing, and it registers the payload formats from the RTP audio and video profile.
tldr.outcome: The registrations let a MIME type name and its parameters be translated into the fields of a Session Description Protocol session description. RFC 3555 was obsoleted by RFC 4855 and RFC 4856.

facts.label: Name case
facts.value: Case-insensitive in both MIME subtypes and RTP encoding names

today: RFC 3555 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 4855 and RFC 4856, and it was updated by RFC 3625 and RFC 4629.

sections.title: Why Payload Formats Need MIME Names
sections.content:
The MIME registration procedure described in RFC 2048 was originally designed for transporting multimedia information over asynchronous Internet mail. The MIME namespace now provides identification for other transport modes as well. This document defines the procedure for registering MIME subtype names for use with the Real-time Transport Protocol, RFC 3550, so that an RTP payload format can be identified in a text-based format or control protocol.

The document also registers all the RTP payload formats defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences, RFC 3551, as MIME subtypes under the audio and video MIME types. Some of these may also be used for transfer modes other than RTP.

The MIME subtype audio/L16 had already been registered through RFC 2586 for transports other than RTP. That registration is incorporated here and augmented with the extra information needed for RTP transport.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP labels a stream with a number, and the number alone does not say which codec is in use. MIME names are already used everywhere else to say what a body of data is, so this RFC registers an RTP payload format as a MIME subtype and gives the names a consistent shape.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registering an RTP payload type as a MIME type follows the same procedures as RFC 2048 and uses the registration template from Section 2.8 of that document. Some additional parameters are required to describe how a particular payload format is carried over RTP.

The published specification must describe the encoding and the payload format, usually by reference to an RTP payload format specification RFC, which may be separate or may be the same document as the registration. That specification MUST include the RTP timestamp clock rate, or multiple rates for audio encodings with several sampling rates.

A rate parameter is required when the payload format does not have a fixed RTP timestamp clock rate, and a format may add further required parameters. Most audio formats may carry an optional channels parameter giving the number of audio channels in the transmission. Any format, but most likely an audio format, may carry the optional parameters ptime, the recommended length in milliseconds of media represented by a packet, and maxptime, the maximum amount of media that can be put in one packet, also in milliseconds. Those two parameters are defined in the Session Description Protocol.

Three cases are described. If the type is not yet registered, a new registration is built from the MIME template and its encoding considerations must say how the type is transferred over RTP. If a MIME type already exists for a non-RTP protocol, its encoding considerations are changed to say it can also be transferred over RTP, and any RTP-specific parameters must be marked as applying only to RTP. If an existing MIME type was registered for RTP and is now to be used for a non-RTP protocol, the change runs the other way, and any non-RTP-specific parameters are marked as applying only outside RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration names the format, points at the document that defines it, and lists the values a sender has to state. Four parameters do most of the work: the clock rate, the number of channels, how much media a packet should hold, and how much it may hold at most. The RFC also covers the three cases a new registration can run into, so that an existing name is never quietly redefined.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP Parameters
sections.content:
A MIME media type is written as type/subtype followed by parameters, each written as attribute=value, with the value quoted when it contains special characters.

The information in the media type string maps to fields of the Session Description Protocol, which is commonly used to describe RTP sessions. The MIME type, for example audio, goes in the SDP m= line as the media name. The MIME subtype, which names the payload format, goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name. The general parameters rate and channels also go in a=rtpmap, as the clock rate and the encoding parameters. The parameters ptime and maxptime go in the SDP a=ptime and a=maxptime attributes.

Any payload-format-specific parameters go in the SDP a=fmtp attribute. The set of allowed parameters is defined by the RFC that specifies the payload format and MUST NOT be extended by the MIME subtype registration without a corresponding revision of that specification. The parameters are suggested to be copied directly from the MIME media type string as a semicolon separated list of parameter and value pairs. A format that specifies some other syntax for the fmtp parameters must have its registration say what the parameters are in MIME format and how to map them to the SDP attribute, and the RFC points at the audio/RED registration as the example of that.

The RFC gives the worked example audio/L16; rate=48000; channels=2; ptime=5; emphasis=50-15 for the media type audio/L16 with a rate of 48000, two channels, a packet time of 5 milliseconds and an emphasis value of 50-15, together with the SDP lines m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 97, a=rtpmap:97 L16/48000/2, a=fmtp:97 emphasis=50-15 and a=ptime:5. It also notes that encoding names defined in the RTP profile are commonly shown in upper case and MIME subtypes in lower case, and that these names are case-insensitive in both places.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a MIME type has one place to go in a session description. The type goes in the media line, the subtype and the clock rate and channel count go in the rtpmap attribute, the timing parameters go in their own attributes, and anything specific to the codec goes in the fmtp attribute. The RFC gives a full example so that both sides can translate a type into a description.

sections.title: The Audio and Video Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers the payload formats described in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences as MIME subtypes. The audio types registered are audio/DVI4, audio/G722, audio/G723, audio/G726-16, audio/G726-24, audio/G726-32, audio/G726-40, audio/G728, audio/G729, audio/G729D, audio/G729E, audio/GSM, audio/GSM-EFR, audio/L8, audio/L16, audio/LPC, audio/MPA, audio/PCMA, audio/PCMU, audio/QCELP, audio/RED and audio/VDVI. The video types are video/BT656, video/CelB, video/JPEG, video/H261, video/H263, video/H263-1998, video/H263-2000, video/MPV, video/MP2T, video/MP1S, video/MP2P, video/BMPEG and video/nv.

For most audio formats the RTP timestamp clock rate equals the sampling rate. Some formats operate only at one fixed sampling rate, while others are adjustable. The audio/L16 registration requires a rate parameter, with permissible values for non-RTP transport of 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100 and 48000 samples per second, and it adds optional channels, emphasis and channel-order parameters, plus ptime and maxptime for RTP.

The audio/RED registration shows how a format with its own parameter syntax is handled. It requires a pt parameter holding a comma-separated list of RTP payload types, which has to be a quoted string, and the registration states how that parameter is mapped to the SDP a=fmtp attribute by dropping the parameter name and turning the commas into slashes, so pt="0,5" maps to a=fmtp:99 0/5.
sections.plainLanguage: The bulk of the document is one registration per format, each following the same template: the name, the required and optional parameters, how the data is encoded, and where the format is specified. The audio/RED registration is worth a second look, because that format carries its own parameter syntax and the RFC has to say how it maps onto a session description.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIME subtype registration procedure specified in this document imposes no security considerations of its own. The registrations in the document do not impose security risks either, though some of them state security considerations specific to that registration.

The RFC notes that several audio and video encodings are well suited to hiding data using steganography, and it points to the RTP specification, RFC 3550, for the security considerations of transporting audio and video over RTP, including the use of encryption where confidentiality is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering a name is not itself a security matter, and the RFC says so. It does warn that some encodings are well suited to carrying hidden data, and it points to the RTP specification for how to protect media in transit.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARAMETERS A MIME REGISTRATION MAY CARRY

items.title: rate
items.text: The RTP timestamp clock rate. Required when the format has no fixed rate.

items.title: channels
items.text: How many audio channels are interleaved in the transmission.

items.title: ptime
items.text: The recommended length of media in a packet, in milliseconds.

items.title: maxptime
items.text: The maximum media that can be put in one packet, in milliseconds.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH PART OF A MIME TYPE GOES IN A SESSION DESCRIPTION

data.title: Example mapping
data.code:
audio/L16; rate=48000; channels=2; ptime=5; emphasis=50-15

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 L16/48000/2
a=fmtp:97 emphasis=50-15
a=ptime:5
